after: ## What challenges do exporters and importers face? (3.1.2)
alt: The eleven challenges grouped in three panels: getting goods there (distance, transport, documentation), money and payment (methods of payment, non-payment, currencies, exchange rates, customs duties) and doing business abroad (language, competition, different legal systems).
caption: Name the challenge, then say how it affects the trader’s cost, risk or sales.

after: ## What challenges do exporters and importers face? (3.1.2)
alt: Bars show what a European buyer pays for an A$100 lamp: 80 euros at A$1 = 0.80 euros, 90 euros at 0.90 and 100 euros at 1.00. A falling currency makes exports more competitive; a rising one makes them dearer abroad.
caption: A stronger currency makes exports dearer abroad; a weaker one makes them cheaper (invented figures).

after: ## How do the Balance of Trade and Balance of Payments differ? (3.1.3)
alt: A large box for the Balance of Payments contains three parts: trade in goods, trade in services and financial flows. Only the trade in goods part is the Balance of Trade. Below, a surplus is exports greater than imports and a deficit is imports greater than exports.
caption: The Balance of Trade covers goods only; the Balance of Payments covers everything.

after: ## How do the Balance of Trade and Balance of Payments differ? (3.1.3)
alt: A waterfall chart. The Balance of Trade is 540 − 610 = −70, a deficit. Services add 230 − 150 = +80, giving +10 on goods and services. A net investment inflow of +25 gives a Balance of Payments surplus of +35.
caption: A goods deficit of $70 million is more than covered by services and investment, giving +$35 million.

after: ## How do the Balance of Trade and Balance of Payments differ? (3.1.3)
alt: Six activities linked to the balance they affect: tourists at a hotel are service exports, food imports are visible imports, insuring foreign ships is an invisible export, ecommerce sales abroad are visible exports, a foreign MNC’s factory is an investment inflow, and its profits sent home are an outflow.
caption: Ask whether money flows in or out, and whether it is goods, services or investment.

after: ## Free trade, trading blocs and trade restrictions (3.1.4)
alt: Three panels: a tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price, a quota limits the quantity imported and causes shortages, and an embargo bans trade so it stops completely. Below, a $50 shoe with a 20% tariff costs $50 + $10 = $60.
caption: A tariff taxes, a quota limits and an embargo bans.

after: ## Free trade, trading blocs and trade restrictions (3.1.4)
alt: Three member countries inside a bloc trade freely, while a non-member’s goods meet a common external tariff at the bloc’s edge. Below, four advantages of joining (larger market, cheaper imports, investment, political cooperation) sit beside four disadvantages.
caption: A bloc opens markets between members but brings competition and shared rules.
